newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Zajedno urges protesters to be wary.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Zajedno urges protesters to be wary.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders urged vigilence on their supporters as street protests wound down ahead of a parliament session to overturn vote-rigging by President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling socialists.

Parliament will meet on Tuesday to discuss a specially-written law recognising victories by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition in 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest towns and cities, including Belgrade, in local elections last November.
Milosevic has finally bowed to continuous demonstrations against socialist attempts to keep control of the councils rather than cede any of the power that his party has wielded for half a century.

But, with the numbers at daily protests in Belgrade visibly dwindling, Zajedno leaders are wary in case his request to the government to enact the results of the elections turns out to be yet another feint.
Even when passed, the law could take up to 10 days to be officially promulgated and hardline nationalist leader Vojislav Seselj has vowed to challenge its constitutional legality.
Zajedno leader Vesna Pesic told an independent Belgrade radio station on Saturday: "Some say the law is unconstitutional, some say it isn't.
"But the Zajedno coalition is definitely not pleased with the entire situation - after 80 days of sacrifice, what we are getting is a truly ridiculous way to solve the problem."
Zajedno has said it will end the street demonstrations when the election results are recognised.
An opinion poll by the Belgrade Social Sciences Institute indicated cynicism among most Serbs about both the government and the opposition.
Only a minority believed the opposition would improve their economy or political freedoms and half feared the socialists would never relinquish power peacefully.
Twenty-nine percent thought Zajedno, which contains only one small party, headed by Pesic, committed to recognisable Western-style democracy, could win national elections.
About a third thought that a transfer of power was important and that economic revival and greater political freedom were likely under Zajedno.
Milosevic, fighting for his political survival, ceded the elections after violence in Belgrade last Sunday when riot police clubbed peaceful demonstrators and turned water cannon on them.
A settlement of the dispute would speed Serbia's return to international diplomatic and financial bodies if accompanied by political reforms demanded by Zajedno and the West.
But diplomats say socialist hardliners who fear reform will destroy their grip on power will watch the process carefully and could still intervene against it in the coming months.
The hardliners could either force Milosevic to side with them or oust him to ensure continued socialist supremacy.
